claims.summary: The training treats modality as a separate selection factor. This supplied text-only profile cannot process the required images; it could qualify for a text-only version of the workload if the other stated requirements stayed the same.

Language coverage is independently required. The stipulated English-only profile is insufficient for Spanish cases, although it would meet an English-only workload with the same image, JSON and latency requirements.

All four stipulated constraints are satisfied: image/text input, both languages, schema-valid JSON and 850 ms below 900 ms. The evidence supports evaluating these factors, not claiming this anonymous profile exists as a commercial model or is optimal outside these tests.

The profile provides only prose, so its other strengths do not satisfy the structured-output requirement. It could fit a conversational interface that accepts prose and does not require the declared JSON record.

The guide-linked evaluation unit connects token windows, context design and latency requirements. Calculating the complete 5,900-token envelope leaves G2; combining stage bounds leaves E2. This pair is supported only under the explicitly supplied model profiles and additive planning contract.

E1/G2 preserves all context but needs 800 ms. It would become feasible if the latency allowance increased to at least that supplied bound; the larger context window does not make its embedding stage run faster.

E2/G1 has enough time but too little generator capacity. It could fit a different task whose complete input and reserved output total at most 4,096 tokens; silently discarding required snippets is not allowed here.

E1/G1 also fails the window even though 600 ms meets the latency limit. It would be feasible for a smaller context envelope under the same latency budget. Model size alone is not used to infer quality, price or token behavior.

The function consumes text through an EMBEDDINGS definition to generate a vector representation. This would be useful when preparing the query embedding for retrieval, but that stage cannot substitute for asking the chat endpoint to compose an answer.

The current accepted MODEL_TYPE list contains EMBEDDINGS, not CHAT_COMPLETIONS. A future independently documented model type could change the interface choice; current code cannot invent that value because an endpoint happens to support chat.

The reference's local ONNX Runtime path is developer Preview and still declares MODEL_TYPE = EMBEDDINGS. It could fit an approved local embedding workload with its extra runtime prerequisites, but it is not the configured remote chat-generation operation.

The transport procedure accepts the prepared payload, URL, method and response OUTPUT variable, and the RAG unit demonstrates using it for generation. The stem supplies endpoint compatibility and access; using this interface does not itself guarantee answer quality or provider-schema validation.

The path assignments match the local example, but the missing gate is external AI runtimes enabled. External REST enablement belongs to remote HTTPS inference and would be relevant if LOCATION referred to a remote model rather than these local directories.

The current local ONNX example separately enables Preview and external AI runtimes, then assigns the model directory to LOCATION and library directory to LOCAL_RUNTIME_PATH. The answer completes only the missing pieces under the supplied installed-files and permissions assumptions.

Both path roles are reversed: the selected LOCATION has libraries rather than model/tokenizer artifacts. It would work only if the actual directory contents also changed to match their documented roles, which the supplied inventory explicitly rules out.

The local example requires LOCATION to identify the directory containing model.onnx and tokenizer.json. Naming only a model file does not follow that configuration contract; it would require a different documented runtime accepting an individual file path, not this Preview setup.

UPDATE admits rows satisfying its search condition, so current revision 42 passes >= 41. A lower-bound predicate could serve an intentionally historical selection task, but it does not certify equality with the source snapshot used for this embedding.

Comparing the proposed result with EmbeddingRevision prevents some regressions between completed workers but ignores newer source text. It could be sufficient only under an additional no-intervening-source-change contract, which the observed revision 42 disproves.

The maintenance unit requires embeddings to track source changes; the UPDATE reference permits a condition on the current row. Under the explicitly supplied application revision contract, equality binds this valid vector to the text snapshot that produced it, and the mismatch leaves retry responsibility with the worker.

Nonnull presence is true for the revision-40 embedding and therefore does not reject the race. This condition could intentionally restrict a refresh job to previously populated rows, but cannot establish freshness against SourceRevision.

The training describes triggers as adding work to writes, including possible immediate generation. That could fit a small workload explicitly prioritizing immediate completion, but conflicts with this asynchronous, low-code cross-system requirement.

The current unit specifically describes Logic Apps checking changed rows, calling an embedding service and coordinating other systems through a low-code workflow. Scheduling is acceptable here; the answer does not assert a connector, cadence, freshness SLA or delivery guarantee not given in the problem.

SQL-triggered Azure Functions can react externally and scale separately, so this is technically relevant rather than impossible. It would fit a code-managed maintenance service, but does not satisfy the stipulated low-code/no-custom-function deployment condition.

Foundry supports model selection or hosting while another process handles change detection and database updates. It could be one component of the selected workflow, but hosting alone cannot satisfy the complete scheduling and notification requirement.

The documented composition associates chunks with each source and passes c.chunk to the embedding operation. Joining by document fixes the row association but leaves d.Body as the represented text. Whole-document generation could be appropriate for one row per whole document, not this per-chunk contract.

Passing c.chunk correctly represents the stored chunk text. The remaining CROSS JOIN still forms every document/chunk pair, contrary to the original per-source CROSS APPLY relationship. Such a Cartesian product could be intentional for a comparison matrix, not source ownership.

Deduplicating projected rows cannot infer which document owned each chunk, and still invokes the model on d.Body. DISTINCT can remove genuinely repeated identical records after a correct mapping, but it does not repair either semantic defect in this pipeline.

The chunks reference demonstrates per-source CROSS APPLY and embedding c.chunk; the generation reference confirms the source expression determines what is sent. Restoring the DocumentId relationship and using that chunk's text preserves both required invariants. This is static relational/code reasoning, not a claimed SQL execution.

The sources distinguish tokenized model limits from text preparation size. The supplied corpus disproves the assumed ratio; a fixed character policy could be accepted only after an actual conservative token-bound validation and a separate boundary-quality check.

Both sources connect input limits with chunking and explain that overly small chunks lose context. Model-aware token checks plus tested boundaries or overlap address the two independent observations. No particular tokenizer API, optimal chunk length or guaranteed quality improvement is asserted.

The documented workflow prepares text before model generation. Scaling a completed vector cannot alter the text request that exceeded the input limit, nor recover words excluded from that request. Scale normalization can be relevant to later vector comparison, after valid inputs have been generated.

The unit warns that chunks that are too small lose important context. Single-word chunks could serve an isolated-term task, but the stated handbook task requires preserving a restriction together with the sentence it modifies.

The documented generation and query pattern use a chosen model for both source and query embeddings. Given the explicit incompatible-space and full-corpus requirements, a complete separately generated snapshot and coordinated cutover preserve those invariants. If storage were constrained, another rollout would need to explicitly preserve them rather than mixing vectors.

The type reference establishes a fixed component count, not semantic interchangeability. A mixed comparison could be justified only if the models were independently established to share a compatible space; the supplied model contract expressly says they do not.

Normalization preserves a vector's direction and changes its length. That can address a scale convention within a compatible space, but cannot establish the different coordinate relationship that this migration explicitly lacks.

Generating B vectors in place can be valid for an offline migration or a service that permits partial coverage. Searching only completed rows during this backfill violates the explicit entire-corpus requirement even though the remaining comparisons are within B's space.

The function generates stored outputs, so row and null counts can measure how much work remains. They are not the documented request/status/error fields needed to distinguish failures of the two remote models.

Norms characterize vector scale and can diagnose a normalization policy after vectors exist. They cannot reveal the HTTP status of an endpoint call that failed during generation; the failure requires transport/model observability.
VECTORPROPERTY returns Dimensions or BaseType, which is useful for a type or dimension investigation. Those properties do not include a model call identifier, HTTP status or error details.

The current function reference explicitly names ai_generate_embeddings_summary for status, errors and model name and external_rest_endpoint_summary for additional REST diagnostics. This is the relevant evidence source; actual event-session setup and handling of potentially sensitive diagnostic data remain implementation work.

The full-text unit distinguishes quoted phrase conditions from separate terms and linguistic expansion. Under the stated populated English index, CONTAINS with the quoted phrase matches the first screen's contract; this is not binary identifier equality or a universal tokenizer claim.

Semantic comparison can find different phrasings, which is useful for the second screen but cannot enforce exact word presence for the first. It becomes appropriate when conceptual similarity, rather than an indexed lexical phrase, is the intended criterion.

The selection unit identifies meaning-oriented retrieval, and VECTOR_DISTANCE supplies exact comparison of compatible query/stored vectors. This fits discovery without promising that a given threshold or ranking is universally relevant.

The unit describes FREETEXT's automatic linguistic expansion, which differs from the explicitly quoted phrase condition. It could fit a broader word-form search, but not this screen's exact-phrase requirement.

The sources describe relevance fusion and numerical similarity, not enforcing stock/market predicates by embedding them. Such labels could contribute useful descriptive meaning, but cannot replace current relational eligibility conditions.

Filtering after an ordered TOP cannot restore rows excluded by that TOP. This could be acceptable for a display-only safety filter when underfilled pools are tolerated, but violates the explicit requirement that ineligible rows consume no branch budget.

The hybrid unit recommends filtering before fusion, and TOP binds the selected ordered rows in its query scope. Applying mandatory predicates before each exact/lexical branch's cap preserves eligible candidate capacity without mistaking RRF for a hard-rule mechanism.

Hybrid fusion retains candidates from either source, so restricting only one branch leaves the vector-only path able to introduce ineligible rows. One-sided filtering could fit enrichment where the other branch is independently guaranteed eligible, a guarantee absent here.

The training distinguishes a simple term from a quoted prefix term with an asterisk. Searching for calib alone would be appropriate if that complete indexed word were required, but does not express all words starting with it.

The unit contrasts LIKE character patterns with full-text token searches. The supplied precalibration text contains the substring calib, so this condition admits a row outside the prefix requirement; it could fit an intentionally anywhere-in-text substring search.

The training demonstrates quoted prefix terms, and CONTAINSTABLE's shared CONTAINS grammar defines the word-star prefix form. Under the explicit indexed-token premise, this matches calibrated and calibration without requiring sensor or matching interior precalibration.

The prefix part is correct, but the supported AND condition also requires sensor and would exclude the required calibration guide. It would suit a narrower query explicitly requiring both the prefix family and sensor, not this one.

CONTAINSTABLE documents KEY as the full-text unique key and warns that top_n_by_rank plus other predicates can underfill results. The TOP reference binds a cap to its query's ORDER BY. Correcting the join and moving the limit after the published filter satisfies all three supplied requirements.

The key repair is correct, but the reference's prelimit warning applies exactly: the function's five selected hits are stipulated to be unpublished. Keeping a global five-hit pool could fit a workflow that accepts later underfill; it cannot provide the required published top five.

Removing the limit addresses candidate loss but not identity. Joining KEY to PaperId would be appropriate if PaperId were the full-text key; the stem explicitly assigns that role to SearchKey, so the remaining mapping is unsupported.

The reference separates KEY from relevance RANK. KEY ordering could satisfy a key-ordered administrative listing, but does not implement the specified descending relevance order with a PaperId tie-break after filtering.

The reference supplies four-byte float32 components; the stipulated count makes this 368,640,000 bytes or 351.5625 MiB. It would be viable with a sufficiently larger component budget, but a quality score above the floor does not waive storage constraints.

1,024 is within the native dimension range, 60,000 × 1,024 × 4 is 234.375 MiB, and the supplied score 92 exceeds 91. This is a workload-specific selection using given measurements, not a product-model claim or a complete storage estimate.

768 dimensions fit the native type and use only 175.78125 MiB of components, but the measured quality is insufficient. It could fit a different workload accepting the lower score; storage savings alone cannot establish retrieval quality.

The current native vector maximum is 1,998 dimensions, so this supplied 2,048-component output cannot be stored unchanged in that type. A separately validated lower-width model configuration or another storage contract would be a different design, not silent truncation of these vectors.

The index reference describes indexing vector values, while the maintenance unit separately requires regeneration after text changes. Recreating an index can help after a large distribution change or old-format migration, but unchanged obsolete vectors remain obsolete.

ALLOW_STALE_VECTOR_INDEX addresses writes with earlier index formats when stale search results are tolerated. The scenario already has latest-format DML support and healthy maintenance; that older setting does not create a new embedding from Body.

A metric computes distances between the supplied vectors. Changing it can serve a differently validated similarity objective, but does not transform the stored old-text vector into the representation of newly committed text.

The generation function creates the representation and the maintenance workflow decides when to replace it. Persisting the new vector supplies actual vector DML for the latest index to maintain. The answer does not claim this alone solves worker races or guarantees search relevance.

The current reference explains that DacPac/BACPAC schema-first import tries vector-index creation before loading data and fails. Keeping an ordinary schema object in an artifact can be appropriate, but this vector-index requirement makes post-import generation too late.

The documented workaround excludes the vector index from import and recreates it after data arrives. Counting at least 100 nonnull vectors satisfies the separate creation minimum under the supplied supported region and valid clustered-key assumptions.

The reference measures the creation minimum in rows containing nonnull vectors. This plan would become valid only after at least five more real embeddings are populated; the 35 null-vector rows do not qualify.

The index needs its minimum data before creation, not eventually afterward. Creating a conventional empty-table index may be a familiar deployment pattern, but is not the current vector-index lifecycle contract.

The reference explicitly returns an integer dimension count for the Dimensions property. Reading that property for each input meets the diagnostic requirement; it does not identify the embedding model or verify cross-model semantic compatibility.

VECTOR_NORMALIZE changes scale to a unit norm and returns a vector. It is appropriate when a known comparison policy requires normalization, not when the required output is metadata counts with no rescaling.
BaseType is a valid metadata property, but its result is a type name rather than a dimension count. It would answer an element-storage-type question, which is a separate diagnostic.
VECTOR_DISTANCE returns one scalar distance under a chosen metric, not two component counts. It belongs after compatible inputs have been established and a pairwise similarity measurement is wanted.

The training defines ANN recall against the exact neighbor set. Fast shares two and three IDs with the respective five-neighbor baselines, giving mean 0.5. It could suit a workload explicitly accepting that measured loss, but not this 0.8 gate.

Exact search is the comparison baseline and has recall 1 against itself, but the supplied 110 ms result fails the latency ceiling. It would become eligible with a larger budget or separately demonstrated faster exact execution, not by assuming a universal size threshold.

Wide matches both exact lists in this fixture, but 95 ms is above the allowed 90 ms. Its result could be appropriate under a relaxed latency target; matching two lists is not evidence of universal ANN recall 1.

Balanced has four shared IDs out of five for each case, so mean recall is exactly 0.8 and 75 ms meets the independent latency condition. The Preview feature and measured configurations are explicitly scoped; no undocumented index tuning parameter is invented.

The function returns negative dot product, so descending order prefers the smaller raw products in this fixture. That ordering would fit a task intentionally selecting the least dot-similar items, not the stipulated relevance contract.

Dot is a supported index metric, and the exact function maps raw products 4,3,1 to -4,-3,-1. Ascending distance therefore yields A,B,C as required. The exact check does not claim to execute through the index or force an ANN physical plan.

Cosine compares direction instead of the required unnormalized product; here B aligns perfectly with q while A has the highest raw dot product. Cosine would be appropriate for a separately validated angle-only model objective, not this magnitude-sensitive one.

Euclidean distances prioritize geometric closeness, putting C before B and A for these supplied coordinates. That is a legitimate different metric but would require a different scoring contract than larger unnormalized q·v.

The current vector reference explicitly requires a subquery for aggregation and multiple ordering columns. An inner distance-ordered approximate cap defines the requested document pool; the outer grouping and top-three ordering then operate on category counts, preserving both levels of the specification.

The approximate-query layer cannot directly combine the stated grouping and count/category ordering. Such aggregation is valid after wrapping the candidate query, or in an ordinary relational query without the approximate clause, but not in this single layer.

Per-category candidate pools answer a different question and can include documents that were outside the global twenty. This could be a useful balanced-per-category report, but it does not count categories within the one global pool specified here.

An inner three-row cap counts documents rather than final categories, and the extra Category ordering key violates the current approximate restriction. An outer tie-break is allowed, but cannot retroactively restore the missing seventeen candidate slots.

The reference states that no-index execution scans with kNN, and forcing ANN requires an index. Dropping it can be useful to establish a no-index baseline but cannot force the ANN strategy requested here.
The current reference explicitly describes TOP plus distance ordering without APPROXIMATE as exact kNN. That is useful as an exact comparison run, not as the forced-ANN benchmark.

The table-hints section supplies WITH (FORCE_ANN_ONLY) on the VECTOR_SEARCH alias and requires an index plus TOP WITH APPROXIMATE. The stem supplies the current platform, index and metric prerequisites; the hint controls strategy, not a latency or recall guarantee.
The METRIC contract requires the same column and metric for compatible ANN use. A mismatch can demonstrate fallback behavior, but removes rather than forces the intended approximate strategy.

The TOP reference states that unordered TOP chooses an undefined subset, and illustrates why outer ordering cannot control an earlier selection. Final sorting is appropriate for presentation only after each limited pool has been correctly chosen.

These branch orders follow full-text and vector relevance directions, but the unordered five-row fusion CTE can still discard higher RRF scores. It would suffice only if F had no limiting TOP or had its own correct ordering.

RANK's OVER order assigns positions while the whole query's order determines returned ordering. Correcting the fusion limit cannot restore better hits lost from unordered branch TOPs; the branch windows are not query-level ORDER BY clauses.

Binding TOP and ORDER BY together at all three scopes preserves the best lexical pool, best exact-vector pool and best fused pool. The chosen scores follow the training's directions, with the generic TOP and RANK references resolving its incomplete sample ordering.

The division reference explicitly truncates integer/integer fractions, so a later decimal cast receives zeros. That late cast would preserve a quotient only if the operands already produced noninteger division; these literals and rank columns do not.

The training uses 1.0 in each division and independently coalesces missing list contributions to 0.0. This preserves a present list's fractional value and gives no score to absence, exactly matching the stipulated RRF arithmetic.

The training's separate COALESCE calls retain one-sided contributions. Wrapping only the sum loses that distinction when either nullable rank is absent; it would coincide with the desired calculation only for rows present in both lists.

Missing lists contribute zero in the source pattern, not the reciprocal for a fictional rank zero. Rank substitution could be part of a separately defined prior-score policy, but it changes the RRF contract being implemented here.

The training defines recall over all relevant documents. One relevant result out of the stated four gives 0.25 for both queries, so fast keyword-only execution cannot pass the 0.5 recall gate; it could fit a lower-recall or different-query task.

Vector-only finds two of four relevant documents and has first relevant ranks two and one, yielding recall 0.5 and MRR 0.75. It would tie without the supplied latency tie-break, but 90 ms loses to hybrid-ten's 75 ms.

Hybrid-ten also finds two of four with first relevant ranks one and two, so its recall and MRR match vector-only. It meets the latency ceiling and wins the explicitly ordered tie-break. The source supports these metrics and measured parameter evaluation, not a universal ten-candidate recommendation.

The larger pool produces three relevant results and first-hit rank one for both fixtures, but its 140 ms measurement violates a hard gate. It could be selected under a relaxed latency policy; improved relevance cannot silently override the current budget.

The training contrasts request-time retrieval with relying on a training snapshot. Fine-tuning can serve a different adaptation goal, but the explicitly frozen/no-retrieval plan cannot incorporate later policy edits or identify request-specific source records.

A cached summary could be useful if it were maintained under a validated freshness/provenance contract. This alternative is explicitly unversioned and reused after edits, so it does not meet the request-specific current-record requirement.

The unit motivates RAG when general models lack the organization's current domain knowledge. Pretrained-only answers can suit stable general knowledge, but cannot establish the actual policy records required for this application.

The source's retrieve-augment-generate pattern supplies relevant database records at request time and permits tracing the context. Retaining source identifiers is the application's explicit design choice; no privacy, model compliance or automatic update guarantee is implied.

The constructor reference documents JSON escaping and nested arrays/objects, and the prompt unit uses role/content messages. This expression preserves the supplied string values in the exact stipulated request shape before transport. It does not prove the model follows the system instruction.

The constructor exists to serialize values with the required escaping; directly concatenating @user into quoted JSON syntax leaves its quote, backslash and control character unescaped. Manual construction could work with correctly encoded values, but no such encoding is performed in this expression.

This is valid JSON construction but produces an object keyed by system/user, not the specified messages array. It could fit a different adapter schema accepting that object, but not the endpoint contract supplied in the question.

JSON_QUERY extracts the context array as a JSON fragment, whereas this endpoint requires user.content to be the prepared string containing context and question. An array-valued context field can be valid for a different explicitly supported schema, but does not satisfy this text-message contract.

The procedure documents @headers as flat JSON and @payload as the body. Header metadata is appropriate for content type or other supported request headers, but a nested messages request cannot replace the body by being placed there.

The prompt unit creates the request body and the transport reference sends it through @payload, with POST and an OUTPUT variable for the reply. The preconfigured endpoint and authentication remain prerequisites; this assignment does not validate provider content or answer quality.

The reference treats the URL and payload as different inputs with different size limits. Query parameters can carry parameters accepted by an endpoint, but the stated chat endpoint contract requires this JSON as the body, not appended URL text.

@response OUTPUT is the destination for received data. It would be relevant after the request to parse the result, but initializing it does not supply the outgoing @payload or change the endpoint's request-body contract.

The reference reserves WITHOUT_ARRAY_WRAPPER for a single-row object and otherwise defaults to an array. This choice might fit one row without a named root when missing null fields are acceptable, but fails all three stated shape requirements.

ROOT supplies the named object and default formatting retains the rows array, but NULL properties are omitted without INCLUDE_NULL_VALUES. This could fit a sparse-context schema where absent and null are equivalent; this consumer explicitly distinguishes them.

INCLUDE_NULL_VALUES fixes null preservation, but the wrapper removal and missing ROOT still conflict with the two-row rooted-array contract. It would be suitable for a different single-object output that retained null fields.

The reference defines each option independently: default array for multiple rows, ROOT for items and INCLUDE_NULL_VALUES for Note:null. The result encodes the supplied rows faithfully without claiming that serialization forces the model's interpretation.

The procedure's zero return represents received 2xx status, whereas the RAG unit separately parses content. A success-only shortcut could be safe only under an independently enforced always-answer response contract; this supplied 204 fixture disproves that assumption.

The reference distinguishes received non/2xx statuses from being unable to make an HTTPS call, which throws. A transport-exception path would be appropriate for no completed call, not this explicit received 204 response.

The reference explicitly omits result for a 204 response while treating 2xx as successful transport. The application must inspect its required answer contract separately before marking generation complete; this does not invent an answer or misreport the transport result.

The response metadata and result payload are separate envelope members. Here the HTTP status is present and clear. Missing status capture would be a different malformed/missing-envelope problem, not a consequence of an intentionally absent 204 body.

The reference separates database/pool outbound throttling from documented retryable HTTP responses. Eight calls exceed the four available slots; retries do not raise the capacity. This launch pattern would require eight available slots, not the supplied reservation.

The transport reference recommends grouping rows into JSON when the endpoint supports batching. Forty requests at five per body require eight calls, and the fixed reservation leaves four concurrent slots. This satisfies both stipulated constraints without inventing a chat-model batch API or a completion-time guarantee.

The concurrency count is feasible, but the supplied gateway contract caps each body at five independent requests. Ten-request batches could be considered only after the gateway explicitly supports that larger shape; SQL payload capacity alone is not that approval.

The procedure's timeout controls how long a call may run, not the concurrent-worker limit. Single-request calls can be appropriate for a nonbatch endpoint, but this endpoint permits batching and forty concurrent calls violate the stated database capacity.

The response unit locates message.content, JSON_VALUE extracts the explicitly short scalar, and OPENJSON can then parse that extracted text. Its typed WITH contract requires nvarchar(max) AS JSON for the citations array. This is a two-layer parse, not a claim that every provider returns this shape.

JSON_QUERY extracts an actual object or array at its input path; the outer content token here is a string. This approach would fit a different envelope whose content member was itself an object, not the escaped JSON string supplied here.

The parser traverses the JSON structure it is given, not a second document hidden in a scalar's characters. Direct content.answer traversal would be correct for object-valued content, but the supplied outer token first requires string extraction and another parse.

OPENJSON's ordinary typed columns extract scalar values, while AS JSON retains an object/array fragment. Omitting AS JSON could be correct if citations were a scalar identifier or string; the supplied value is the array [17,23] that must remain intact.

The retrieved design unit recommends meaningful input for the actual retrieval task. DisplayName carries the stipulated brand, but this pair drops the feature description and includes an explicitly opaque irrelevant key. It could fit a different task where the key had semantic meaning and features were unnecessary.

Description carries features but omits the stipulated brand-bearing name, while ModifiedAt is expressly operational here. A recency-focused task could need that date in its context, but this brand-and-feature semantic-input contract does not.

The two specified semantic requirements reside in DisplayName and Description. Choosing both follows the source's task-specific input guidance and excludes only fields the stem expressly deems irrelevant; it is not a universal rule that all identifiers and dates lack meaning.

Neither the opaque key nor the operational timestamp supplies the required brand-and-feature content. They can be useful metadata for storage, lineage or filtering, but not replacements for the stated embedding input.

The newly retrieved maintenance unit says Change Tracking records that a row changed since a point in time and can drive background refresh batches. That fits this changed-row signal with current-text reads; it does not provide a complete checkpoint-retention, retry or exactly-once implementation.

CDC's detailed before/after change information is the distinction the stem deliberately excludes. CDC could be chosen when detailed change values are required; being asynchronous does not make it the requested lighter changed-row mechanism here.

A table trigger can mark or initiate refresh and can support a custom change log, but the requirement explicitly avoids building one. A trigger could fit immediate marking or an intentionally custom write-path mechanism under different operational constraints.

The current unit assigns Foundry model selection/hosting a supporting role while another process detects database changes and writes embeddings. It can participate in the system, but model management alone is not the specified row-change mechanism.

The current product reference explicitly states that VECTOR_DISTANCE is exact and does not use a vector index even when one exists. True is the function-contract answer on the specified SQL Server 2025 platform; exact does not mean infinite numerical precision or guaranteed execution speed.

Index existence does not make this function approximate, so False contradicts the current contract. A separate VECTOR_SEARCH operation can use a compatible ANN index, but that alternate operation does not alter the assertion about VECTOR_DISTANCE.

Under the supplied mathematical RRF formula A contributes only 1/21, below B's 2/22. A could outrank B under a differently weighted or differently ranked input, but rank one in one list has no absolute priority in the stated sum.
The two lists have equal contribution formulas here, so C also has only 1/21. A separately specified vector weight could favor C, but this formula includes no automatic vector-first rule.

A and C do tie at 1/21, but B's two rank-two contributions are larger. Their tie would be the highest if B were absent or had a sufficiently lower supplied score; neither condition holds in the given data.

B receives 1/22 from each list and sums to 2/22, which exceeds 1/21. This is the explicitly stated real-valued mathematical formula, not an executable T-SQL expression with integer operands, and its supplied k is not a universal default or optimum.

The current training combines unique-per-list IDs with a FULL OUTER JOIN and coalesces the output ID and absent contributions. With the stated uniqueness premise, this retains keyword-only, vector-only and shared documents without a many-to-many fanout.

An inner join keeps only shared IDs; substituting zero after the join cannot recover removed one-sided documents. That intersection would be appropriate if both retrieval methods had to agree, but not for the supplied union-style candidate contract.

A keyword-side left join preserves its own unmatched documents but loses vector-only IDs. It could fit lexical-first enrichment when vector-only discoveries are deliberately excluded, which is not this requirement.

A cross join produces every pair rather than merging equal document IDs. It is useful for an intended all-pairs comparison, but does not implement one output per candidate across the two unique-key lists.

PATH mode interprets the dotted aliases as nested properties, so these flat dotted-key names are not the shown query's output. A serializer expressly using literal dotted keys could produce this other shape, but that is not FOR JSON PATH's selected convention.

The nesting is correct, but the default array remains because WITHOUT_ARRAY_WRAPPER is absent. This shape could follow an explicitly requested single-row object wrapper removal, not the shown statement.

The directly fetched product contract combines dotted-alias nesting with the default array wrapper even for one row. The supplied literal values therefore form one nested item object inside the array; this is a serialization result, not evidence of downstream model compliance.
An items root would require an explicit ROOT('items') option. That option could create the proposed outer wrapper in a different statement, but it is not present here.

The supplied response wraps choices under result, so the path omitting that level cannot locate the answer. It would fit a variable containing the unwrapped provider result, not the complete envelope shown.

The current response unit demonstrates the exact result.choices[0].message.content path and scalar JSON_VALUE extraction. The given short string and fixed envelope make the choice bounded; no arbitrary-length or all-provider response claim is added.

The unit differentiates JSON_QUERY for an object/array from JSON_VALUE for a scalar. JSON_QUERY would suit object- or array-valued content in a different documented contract, but the supplied content is a short scalar string.
This path addresses the HTTP status code in the envelope, not the assistant's answer text. It is useful for transport diagnostics, a distinct task from extracting the given model message.
Dividing [-3,4] by the absolute-value sum seven gives this norm1 result. It would be correct for norm1, but the shown expression explicitly requests Euclidean norm2.
Dividing by the maximum absolute component four yields the norminf result. That is another documented norm, not the norm2 denominator requested by the statement.

The current reference defines norm2 as the square root of squared components: sqrt(9+16)=5. Scaling [-3,4] by that denominator yields approximately [-0.6,0.8] with the same direction, allowing ordinary floating-point rounding.

The unscaled input has Euclidean length five and is not the requested unit vector. It could be the output of selecting the original variable without normalization, but not the shown successful norm2 operation.

The current reference retains earlier-index TOP_N post-filter semantics: the five nearest candidates are selected before the predicate. Because all five supplied candidates fail Approved=1, the result is empty; this explanation is limited to the expressly earlier index version.

Metric incompatibility can produce a warning and kNN fallback, but the stem explicitly fixes a matching compatible index. It would be a separate diagnostic if the metric or column differed, not an explanation for this earlier-index candidate loss.
An ambiguous distance reference can cause an error according to the current alias rules. This query completes with an empty set, so an execution-stopping ambiguity is a different failure mode.

The function requires a base table and does not support a view as its TABLE input. That restriction matters for an invalid source object, but the given valid base-table query completed successfully and is instead losing its already selected candidates to filtering.

Changing the query to cosine can make it compatible with the existing cosine index, but violates the application's explicit Euclidean requirement. It is viable only for a separately justified change to the model's metric contract.

kNN fallback can execute a Euclidean query without a compatible ANN index. It is a valid exact alternative, but intentionally keeping the fallback does not supply the requested ANN compatibility prerequisite.
The reference requires the same column as well as metric. A Euclidean index on another vector column can help queries against that column, but does not match this Embedding query.
